title: Root: vērus (true) — asserting it, having it, faking it
core: All three descend from Latin *vērus*, "true," but each fastens onto a different link in the chain between a fact and the person reporting it. One is the act of putting a claim forward as true; one is the property of being true (and of being the kind of source that tells the truth); one is the mere look of truth, which can sit on something entirely false. All three are formal enough that they signal courtroom, criticism, or reportage rather than ordinary speech.

words.nuance: The only verb here — an **act**, not a quality. **Aver** is the moment a speaker stakes their own credibility on a statement, usually against doubt: it says nothing about whether the claim is true, only that the person refuses to hedge. Its object is always a proposition (*averred that…*), never a text or a performance.

The **actual** truth-value, and the trait of a habitual truth-teller. Alone in this group it can be predicated of a person as a standing virtue, and it is the only one that presumes real correspondence to fact — which is why it lives in the negative: what gets *questioned* or *disputed* is whether the claim is genuinely true, not whether it sounds true.

Appearance only, and deliberately silent about fact — a forgery or a lie can have plenty of it. It attaches to **made things** (a novel, a set, a performance, an alibi) and is critics' cool praise for craft; you cannot verisimilitude a claim or possess it as a character trait.

exam_note: The trap is treating **verisimilitude** as a synonym for truth — in sentence equivalence it pairs with *plausibility* and *lifelikeness*, and a context conceding something is fabricated still supports it, where **veracity** would be wrong.
